- If sentiment is consistently neutral or negative (0.00), model tends to overestimate prices; correct by reducing forecast by 2–5% relative to peak or mean.
- After sharp price spikes (e.g., >10% from prior day), model often overshoots and fails to correct; apply downward bias of 3–8% for 3–5 days post-spike.
- When sentiment shows early positive signals (e.g., 0.20–0.33), model tends to overreact; reduce forecast slope or cap upward movement to avoid overcorrection.
- If history shows strong mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 consecutive days of decline), model often fails to recognize it; adjust forecast to align with recent 7–14 day moving average.
- For 30-day forecasts, model often underestimates volatility in low-sentiment periods; increase forecast variance or add 1–3% upward buffer if sentiment remains flat.
- If sentiment is positive but recent prices are falling, model may misread trend; apply downward correction to avoid “false optimism” bias.
- In multi-day consecutive low sentiment (e.g., 3+ days of 0.00), model tends to underestimate true drop; add 1–5% downward adjustment to forecast.
- If model shows steady upward trend but true outcome shows sharp drop, sentiment may be misleading; check sentiment for 3–5 days prior to adjust downward.
